lessons.title: Burn Rate and Runway: Cash Planning for Startups

children.text: A startup that is not yet profitable has one number that governs everything: how many months of cash are left. Every other metric, growth, retention, pipeline, is a story about the future. Runway is the deadline by which that story has to become true. This lesson is written for founders and for the people who work alongside them, because in a startup the cash conversation is not confined to the finance team.

body.text: Runway is a date, not a number. Write it on the wall as a month, because every hiring decision, every campaign and every vendor contract either moves that date closer or pushes it away.

children.text: Gross Burn, Net Burn, Runway
Three definitions, and people mix up the first two constantly, usually in their own favour.

body.latex: \text{Net burn} = \text{Cash out} - \text{Cash in} \qquad \text{Runway (months)} = \frac{\text{Cash in bank}}{\text{Net burn per month}}
body.caption: Gross burn is total cash spent. Net burn is what actually leaves after revenue arrives

children.text: LedgerLoop is a fictional Bengaluru B2B software company, eighteen months old, with ₹6 crore in the bank after a seed round.

body.caption: LedgerLoop: one month of cash (₹ lakh)

cells: 22 people, including PF, ESI and gratuity provisioning
Total cash leaving the business every month
Cash actually received, not invoices raised
What the bank balance falls by each month

stats.label: Runway
stats.context: Cash-out month is roughly this time next year

body.text: Use cash collected, not revenue booked. A startup billing ₹45 lakh a month and collecting ₹30 lakh is burning ₹50 lakh, not ₹35 lakh. Founders who calculate runway on booked revenue routinely discover they have two or three months less than they thought, and they discover it late.

body.title: Which burn matters for runway
body.textWithBlank: Runway is calculated by dividing cash in the bank by the ___ burn, which is cash out less cash in.
body.explanation: Gross burn tells you what the business costs to run. Net burn tells you how fast the bank balance falls, which is what sets the deadline. As revenue grows, gross burn can rise while net burn falls, and that is exactly what a business moving towards profitability looks like.

children.text: Every Decision Moves the Date

The board meeting proposes hiring 8 engineers at ₹1.5 lakh a month each to accelerate the roadmap. Finance proposes a cost reduction instead. Here is what each does to the deadline, with the same ₹6 crore in the bank.

body.caption: The same ₹6 crore, three different deadlines

cells: Payroll rises by ₹12 lakh a month
Marketing ₹12 lakh to ₹5 lakh, tools ₹8 lakh to ₹6 lakh, admin ₹10 lakh to ₹8 lakh

children.text: Eight hires cost 2.3 months of runway. That is not an argument against hiring, it is the actual price of the decision, and it should be stated in months in the meeting where the decision is made, not discovered in a spreadsheet a quarter later.

body.text: Notice which lever is largest. Salaries are ₹50 lakh of an ₹80 lakh gross burn, so no combination of tool cancellations and travel policies will move the date much. In a startup, burn is headcount, and every serious runway decision is ultimately a headcount decision.

body.title: Work out the deadline
body.prompt: A startup has ₹4.5 crore in the bank. It spends ₹65 lakh a month and collects ₹20 lakh a month in revenue. How many months of runway does it have? Round to the nearest whole month.
body.explanation: Net burn is ₹65 lakh minus ₹20 lakh, which is ₹45 lakh a month. ₹450 lakh divided by ₹45 lakh is 10 months. If revenue is growing, the true runway is a little longer, which is why a serious founder models a declining burn month by month rather than relying on one division.

children.text: How Much Runway Is Enough

The answer is set by how long raising money takes, not by how comfortable the founder feels. In India a serious institutional round typically takes four to six months from first conversation to money in the bank: meetings, term sheet, diligence, documentation, and then the actual remittance and filings.

body.title: Two founders, same business, different timing

columns.label: Starts raising at 12 months of runway
points: Negotiates from a position of choice
Can walk away from a bad term sheet
If the round fails, there is still time to cut and extend
Investors see planning, which is itself a signal

columns.label: Starts raising at 5 months of runway
points: Every investor conversation is visibly urgent
Terms get worse as the deadline approaches
One slow diligence process becomes existential
Bridge financing from existing investors on their terms
Cuts must be made while raising, which weakens the pitch

body.label: Indian startup funding, 2025
body.context: Tracxn reported Indian tech startups raising roughly $10.5 billion in 2025, down about 17% from $12.7 billion in 2024, with seed funding falling about 30% to $1.1 billion and the number of rounds down nearly 39% to 1,518. Other trackers put the total closer to $11 billion. The direction is what matters: fewer, more selective rounds, which lengthens every raise and makes runway planning a survival skill rather than a spreadsheet exercise.

body.text: Plan the raise backwards from the cash-out date. If a round takes up to six months and you want three months of buffer after it fails, the first investor meeting belongs at around nine to twelve months of runway. Founders who wait until six months are not raising, they are negotiating a rescue.

body.title: Burn multiple: the number investors will ask about

children.text: Runway tells you how long you live. Burn multiple tells you whether the burn is buying anything.

content.latex: \text{Burn multiple} = \frac{\text{Net burn over the year}}{\text{Net new ARR added over the year}}
content.caption: Rupees burned for every rupee of new annual recurring revenue

children.text: LedgerLoop grows monthly revenue from ₹30 lakh to ₹50 lakh over a year, so ARR goes from ₹3.6 crore to ₹6 crore, adding ₹2.4 crore. It burned ₹6 crore to do it, giving a burn multiple of 2.5.
Under 1:
exceptional. Each rupee burned buys more than a rupee of new ARR.
1 to 2:
strong, and fundable in most markets.
2 to 3:
acceptable early, but investors will probe the efficiency.
Above 3:
the business is buying growth expensively, and a funding slowdown makes that dangerous.

The related question from any Indian investor today is payback: how many months of gross margin does it take to recover what you spend acquiring a customer? Under twelve months is comfortable, beyond eighteen is a burn problem wearing a growth costume.

body.title: Six months left
body.question: A founder has 6 months of runway, a round that is not progressing, and a team of 22. Which action extends runway the most and the fastest?
options: Cancel unused software subscriptions and renegotiate the cloud contract
Move the office to a smaller space when the lease renews in four months
Reduce headcount now, protecting the people who directly build and sell the product
Ask customers on monthly plans to switch to annual upfront payment at a discount
body.explanation: Salaries dominate the burn, so only headcount moves the date materially, and delaying that decision shrinks the options rather than saving anyone. Tools and office space are small and slow. The annual upfront switch is genuinely useful and appears in Lesson 2.3, but it brings cash forward at a discount rather than reducing the burn, and it works best before the situation is urgent.

body.title: The hiring plan and the deadline
body.scenario: You are the first finance hire at LedgerLoop: ₹6 crore in the bank, ₹50 lakh net burn, 12 months of runway. The founders want to hire 8 engineers immediately to ship an AI feature they believe will double growth, taking net burn to ₹62 lakh and runway to about 9.7 months. Their argument is that the feature is what makes the next round raisable at a good valuation, and that being cautious now guarantees a mediocre round later.
body.prompt: They are not wrong about the product. How do you structure this decision?
body.modelAnswer:
Reframe the question first.
1. This is not hire or do not hire. It is: does this feature, shipped by month X, raise the probability and price of the next round by more than 2.3 months of runway is worth?
2. Make the cash-out date explicit and put it on the wall. At ₹62 lakh of net burn, the money runs out in about 9.7 months, so the first investor meeting has to happen within roughly three to four months, not after the feature ships.
Then structure it so both things can be true.
3. Stage the hiring. Four engineers now, four after a defined milestone such as the beta shipping or three design partners signing. Half the burn increase, most of the speed.
4. Consider contractors or a specialist agency for the first build. Higher monthly cost, no long-term commitment, and reversible if the round slips.
5. Fund part of it from the burn itself rather than the runway: the cut plan takes ₹11 lakh a month out of marketing, tools and admin, which pays for most of the four hires without touching the deadline.
6. Bring revenue forward. Annual upfront contracts at a modest discount, deposits from design partners, or milestone billing all add cash without adding dilution.
Then set the tripwires before anyone signs an offer letter.
7. Agree now, in writing, what happens at 6 months of runway if the round has not progressed: which costs stop, who is affected, and who decides.
8. Agree the milestone that would justify hiring the second four, and the milestone whose absence would stop it.
9. Start investor conversations immediately in parallel, informally. It costs nothing and it tells you whether the feature thesis actually lands with the people who will fund it.
What I would say plainly.
10. Hiring 8 people with 12 months of runway during a selective funding market is a bet that everything goes right. Staging the same hires costs about a month of speed and removes most of the existential risk. If the founders still want all 8, that is a legitimate choice, but it should be made with the cash-out month written on the whiteboard, not implied.

body.title: The founder's monthly cash review
steps: Record the actual bank balance on the 1st, across every account and deposit.
Calculate gross burn and net burn for the month just ended, using cash collected rather than revenue billed.
Divide the balance by a three-month average net burn, not the single best month, and write down the resulting cash-out month.
Compare that cash-out month with last month's. If it moved closer, name the decision that moved it.
List committed future outflows not in the monthly burn: annual contracts, gratuity, ESOP buybacks, advance tax, statutory dues.
Check the collections list: which customers are late, and how much cash is sitting in unpaid invoices.
Re-run runway on a downside case: revenue flat for six months and one large customer churning.
Confirm the date you must start raising, counting back four to six months from the cash-out month, and diarise it.

cards.definition: Total cash leaving the business each month, before any revenue is counted.
Cash out less cash in. The monthly fall in the bank balance.
Cash in the bank divided by monthly net burn. Best expressed as a calendar month.
The month the money runs out at current burn. Every plan is measured against it.
Net burn divided by net new ARR. How many rupees of cash buy one rupee of new recurring revenue.
Interim funding, usually from existing investors, to reach the next milestone. Terms reflect the urgency.

points: Runway is cash divided by net burn, and it should be stated as a calendar month everyone can see.
Calculate burn on cash collected, not revenue billed, or the deadline arrives earlier than expected.
LedgerLoop's 12 months becomes 9.7 with eight hires and 15.4 with a spending cut. Every decision has a price in months.
Salaries dominate burn, so material runway decisions are headcount decisions. Acting early preserves the choice of who stays.
A round takes four to six months, so start raising at nine to twelve months of runway, and plan backwards from the cash-out date.
Burn multiple shows whether the burn is buying growth. Under 2 is strong, above 3 is expensive growth in a selective market.

body.text: LedgerLoop is fictional and its figures are illustrative. Funding data is from Tracxn as reported for calendar 2025, and other trackers report slightly different totals. Fundraising timelines and burn multiple benchmarks are general market observations, not rules. Nothing here is investment advice.
